video_title: It's a bull market and nobody drinks anymore. | TCAF 255
gist: The Compound and Friends #255 with Strategas ETF strategist Todd Sohn on an industry launching roughly 900 ETFs year-to-date, where a Y Combinator-backed issuer (Corgi) is cloning popular thematics at half the fee, Roundhill's new photonics fund took all the volume from four incumbents in days, and Goldman has bought both Innovator and NEOS to own the buffer and option-income categories aimed at aging demographics. The wider tape: the Lakers at $12.4bn implying Madison Square Garden Sports should be 30-50% higher, $3 trillion of retail money market cash that won't move until Fed funds are below 3%, and a filed pipeline of compute-price ETFs following the Nvidia-Goldman-Apollo-Blackstone $500bn roundtable.

themes.theme: The ETF launch flood and fee compression

insights.claim: Roughly 900 ETFs have launched year-to-date in 2026 against about 1,000-1,100 for all of last year, and Sohn argues this is not temporary because both the cost of launching and the cost of maintaining a fund that never catches on have collapsed.
insights.speaker: Todd Sohn (Strategas)
insights.so_what: Structurally lower launch costs mean supply of product now outruns demand for it — the setup for a wave of quiet closures rather than a slowdown in issuance.

insights.claim: Corgi, a Y Combinator-backed issuer, has launched roughly 30 thematic ETFs cloning the most popular funds at about 35 basis points — half the incumbent cost — plus levered single-stock and index products at 50bp against a typical 90-120bp, explicitly running a Hollywood box-office model where three hits pay for seven flops.
insights.speaker: Todd Sohn (Strategas)
insights.so_what: Venture-funded issuers that don't need each fund to be profitable can undercut incumbent fee structures indefinitely — a direct margin threat to the levered and thematic ETF businesses.

insights.claim: Sohn thinks active thematic ETFs reaching 10 basis points by the end of the decade is not unreasonable, and that incumbents will have to cut prices — especially once cloned funds season and show no tracking difference.
insights.speaker: Todd Sohn (Strategas)
insights.so_what: Fee compression is arriving in the last segment that had escaped it — a revenue headwind for the specialist issuers that have been the industry's growth story.

insights.claim: Five photonics ETFs now exist against roughly three photonics stocks, and Roundhill's fund — only three or four days old — is already doing more volume than the four incumbents combined, demonstrating that brand and distribution decide thematic winners rather than being first.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown and Todd Sohn
insights.so_what: Liquidity concentrates in the branded vehicle regardless of launch order, so first-mover advantage in thematics is worth little — a caution for anyone underwriting new issuers on time-to-market.

insights.claim: The institutional credibility threshold has moved from $100 million to $1 billion of AUM — Sohn says allocators are telling Strategas to call them when its own $890 million fund reaches a billion.
insights.speaker: Todd Sohn (Strategas)
insights.so_what: A 10x rise in the size gate makes the survivorship math for the 900 annual launches brutal — most will never clear the bar to receive institutional money.

insights.claim: There is no enforcement mechanism against cloning: Brown notes that ripping off a product this directly in another industry would end in court, but in ETFs nobody is coming to rescue incumbents from cheaper copies of their own funds.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Product IP is effectively unprotectable in ETFs, which means the durable moat is brand and distribution, not fund design.

insights.claim: Brown concedes he was wrong that direct indexing would slow ETF proliferation — custom indexing turned out to be a high-net-worth wealth management product that retail never wanted, because buying a ticker is simply easier.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Direct indexing's failure to capture retail removes the main structural threat to the ETF wrapper — supporting continued product proliferation.

themes.theme: Goldman's buffer and income land grab

insights.claim: Goldman Sachs acquired both Innovator (defined-outcome buffer ETFs) and NEOS (option income ETFs) for roughly $4 billion combined — about $2.3 billion for NEOS against roughly $30 billion of AUM — buying the two breakout ETF categories of the last two years in one move.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown and Todd Sohn
insights.so_what: A roughly 7-8% of AUM price for an options-based ETF business sets a valuation benchmark for the remaining independent issuers in these categories.

insights.claim: Brown reads the logic as making Goldman's RIA custody push economically viable: custody cannot pay for itself on trade basis points, so the purpose is asset management revenue from products people in their 50s and 60s actually want — yield and downside protection.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Explains the strategy behind Solomon's wealth push and predicts further product acquisitions rather than organic build — watch remaining independents as targets.

insights.claim: Buffer and option-income AUM is described as sticky and non-cyclical — not hot theme money — because the demographic buying it does not sell, which is what makes it worth paying up for.
insights.speaker: Todd Sohn and Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Sticky retiree AUM commands a higher multiple than thematic AUM — the reason these two acquisitions cost more per dollar of assets than a thematic shop would.

insights.claim: Vanguard is notably absent from buffer and option-income categories, and Brown's call is that it will have to build them in-house because that is where the growth is.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Vanguard entering would compress fees in the last high-margin ETF category — the tail risk to Goldman's $4bn of purchases.

themes.theme: Sports franchises as a stock-market derivative

insights.claim: Madison Square Garden Sports carries a roughly $10 billion market cap and $11 billion enterprise value while the Lakers just transacted at $12.4 billion, implying MSGS should trade 30-50% higher even allowing a discount for Dolan's stated unwillingness to sell.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: A concrete public-market arbitrage against a private transaction comp — with a catalyst attached in the Rangers spin-off.

insights.claim: MSG expects to complete a tax-free spin-off of the Rangers business from the Knicks into a separate publicly traded company by the end of October, creating what would effectively be a pure Knicks stock.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: A dated corporate action that would let public investors own a single franchise directly — the mechanism by which the private-public valuation gap could close.

insights.claim: NBA franchise transaction prices have escalated from Ballmer's $2 billion Clippers purchase to Rockets $2.2bn, Nets $3.3bn, Suns $4bn, Trail Blazers $4.25bn, Celtics $6bn and Lakers $10bn now marked at $12.5bn — with Brown arguing the driver is simply the stock market and the wealth of the top 1% of the 1%.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Frames franchise prices as a high-beta derivative of mega-cap equity wealth — meaning a real equity drawdown would hit sports valuations hard and quickly.
insights.quote: This is not people that make made their money in shipping like the Steinbrenners. This is straight up like shareholders in the 100 largest companies in the world.

insights.claim: Sportico's top-10 franchise list — Clippers $7.5bn, Falcons $9.78bn, Knicks $9.9bn, Yankees $9-10bn, Warriors $11.33bn, Giants $12bn, Rams $12.7bn, Cowboys $15.5bn — predates the Lakers transaction, and Brown argues the Cowboys and Yankees are really $20 billion franchises.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Published valuation marks lag transaction prices materially, which is the standing source of arbitrage in any listed sports asset.

insights.claim: The Yankees just completed a $2.6 billion financing agreement with Apollo Sports mixing credit and equity, with no public valuation disclosed.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Private credit is now a primary funding channel for franchises — a growing, under-covered exposure inside alternative asset managers' books.

insights.claim: Brown warns that private equity's enthusiasm for sports — where putting 'sports' on a fund wrapper guarantees a sellout — plus minority-stake churn creates flipping incentives, and proposes a five-year holding period rule to protect fans.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Ownership-structure regulation is the tail risk to the sports-asset trade — leagues can impose holding periods that destroy the liquidity premium PE is underwriting.

insights.claim: Retail money market fund assets stand at $3 trillion against $1.5 trillion the day before the pandemic, and Brown maintains his call that this cash is stuck — arguing it takes Fed funds below 3% to unstick it, since a stock market boom plus higher long rates plus a lower funds rate has not moved it.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: The most-cited bullish 'cash on the sidelines' argument is being falsified in real time — and the specific unlock condition (funds rate below 3%) is testable.

insights.claim: Brown's non-consensus prediction: in a 35% S&P drawdown, money would flow out of money market funds into stocks rather than the reverse — which he says has probably never happened before, because this generation of investors will not run from equities.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: If retail buys a crash rather than selling it, the depth and duration of the next bear market is structurally shorter than history implies.

insights.claim: Korea tightened its market not through interest rates but by banning new 2x single-stock funds and requiring roughly a week of simulated trading before investors can trade levered ETFs — which the hosts characterize as a genuine and different form of monetary tightening.
insights.speaker: Todd Sohn
insights.so_what: A live regulatory template for curbing retail leverage that the US is culturally unlikely to copy — and a reason Korean speculative flows may cool while US flows don't.

insights.claim: Levered long ETF assets reached a $200 billion high water mark with $500 billion of notional exposure, making swap counterparties uncomfortable — yet July's washout cut those assets only about 25%, and Sohn expects the demand for leverage to come straight back.
insights.speaker: Todd Sohn
insights.so_what: A $500bn notional levered complex that barely flinched in a drawdown is a systemic concentration to watch — the counterparty side is where the stress would show first.

insights.claim: Consumer staples have fallen to 4.5% of the S&P 500 and consumer discretionary below 10% — a level Sohn says usually only occurs in tough economic environments — while healthcare went from 16% to 8%, which Brown jokes is healthcare taking a GLP-1.
insights.speaker: Todd Sohn and Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Extreme sector weight compression is partly a denominator effect from mega-cap tech — but discretionary below 10% in a strong economy is a genuine anomaly worth watching.

insights.claim: Energy's beta to the S&P has collapsed to negative at roughly 2% of index weight, which Brown argues makes it a genuine hedge precisely when bonds are not hedging.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: A negative-beta, cash-generative sector at a 2% index weight is an unusually cheap portfolio hedge — a specific, actionable allocation argument.

insights.claim: Sohn frames healthcare as the contrarian setup: bottom-decile relative performance, persistent large outflows from healthcare ETFs and universal dislike — and it is finally starting to work, though the sector is far more dispersed than energy, where stocks move together.
insights.speaker: Todd Sohn
insights.so_what: Sentiment, flows and relative performance all bottomed together — but the dispersion means the sector ETF is a worse expression than stock selection.

insights.claim: Bloom Energy entered the Russell 2000 reconstitution as a roughly $100 billion market cap company — something that has never happened in the index before — which Sohn says makes the next six to twelve months unusually interesting for small caps.
insights.speaker: Todd Sohn
insights.so_what: A single $100bn constituent distorts the entire small-cap benchmark, which means Russell 2000 performance this year may say more about one stock than about small caps.

insights.claim: Money is leaving crypto ETFs and going into AI stocks, with Sohn noting product proliferation got absurd — 2x Dogecoin — and Brown arguing most altcoin ETFs are penny stocks supercharged by Twitter and Reddit rather than a new asset class.
insights.speaker: Todd Sohn and Josh Brown
insights.so_what: The rotation from crypto to AI in ETF flows is the flow-of-funds explanation for crypto's underperformance that Bankless and Michael Howell describe from the liquidity side.

insights.claim: International ETF flows are dead except where AI exposure exists — Korea and Taiwan drove emerging markets while Japan and Europe performed well without attracting interest, with China the persistent disaster.
insights.speaker: Todd Sohn
insights.so_what: Good performance without flows means the international trade is still under-owned — the setup for outsized moves if the AI-only flow filter breaks.

themes.theme: New asset classes: compute, prediction markets, electricity

insights.claim: Multiple compute-price ETFs have already been filed — ProShares, Roundhill and possibly Defiance — following a CNBC roundtable featuring Jensen Huang, David Solomon, Apollo and Blackstone announcing a $500 billion partnership and pitching compute as a new asset class.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown and Todd Sohn
insights.so_what: Compute is being deliberately financialized from the top down — expect futures markets and model-portfolio compute sleeves, and the associated circular-financing risk.

insights.claim: Brown characterizes the roundtable as a circular-financing event dressed as programming — the network gave over its afternoon, everyone on Wall Street watched, and Larry Fink was the only participant who did not attend in person.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: The most senior actors in the AI capex chain publicly cross-guaranteeing each other is precisely the pattern that marks late-cycle financing structures.

insights.claim: Brown's prediction-market ETF thesis draws on Mauboussin and Callahan's paper showing betting markets are accurate one-for-one but exhibit longshot bias — so heavy favorites are structurally underpriced, and a fund systematically buying favorites above roughly 85% implied probability would have a structural edge.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: A genuinely novel, academically-grounded product idea — and Sohn confirms Subversive has already filed, with the SEC currently holding it open for comment.

insights.claim: Harbor Capital is launching actively managed ecosystem ETFs targeting individual AI firms' supply chains — with the largest holding in the OpenAI ecosystem fund being SoftBank — which Brown likes conceptually but expects will not gain traction.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown and Todd Sohn
insights.so_what: Ecosystem funds face the overlap problem — heavy duplication with each other and with plain tech ETFs, which is why the concept rarely survives contact with allocators.

insights.claim: Brown compares AI supply-chain investing to the eras when TV segments disassembled a Dell to point at the Pentium chip and later took apart iPhones to name Skyworks and the glass makers — patterns investors got bored of quickly, and will again.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: A historical base rate for supply-chain thematics: they arrive at peak media interest and decay long before the underlying technology does.

insights.claim: The reason gold ETFs worked and commodity ETFs never did is storage: gold sits in a vault while oil, gas and agricultural products require futures, exposing investors to contango and K-1 partnership tax treatment nobody wants.
insights.speaker: Michael Batnick and Todd Sohn
insights.so_what: A clean structural rule for which physical assets can be securitized cleanly — relevant to whether compute or electricity ETFs can actually deliver spot exposure.

insights.claim: Sohn's fall outlook is that reporting will turn to thematic funds falling on their face — simply because there are too many of them and not enough money to go around — while the underlying equity market remains in a bull market.
insights.speaker: Todd Sohn
insights.so_what: A dated, specific call on the narrative turn — product failure stories arriving while the index still rises, which is a late-cycle rather than bearish signal.

insights.claim: Brown draws a distinction that failed ETFs harm nobody the way failed IPOs do: if the fund tracks what it promised and simply gathers no assets, investors aren't hurt — as with tanker shipping ETFs up a thousand percent that still attracted no money.
insights.speaker: Josh Brown
insights.so_what: Explains why issuance will not self-correct through investor harm — the failure mode is commercial rather than investor loss, so the flood continues.
